hints: Look at butamben and find the atom with an available lone pair that can accept a proton.
walkthrough:
Spot the basic centre**
Picture butamben: you have an aromatic $\text{NH}_2$ group, an ester $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$. Only the amine nitrogen has a lone pair readily available to accept $\text{H}^+$. Acting as a base means exactly that, accepting a proton.

Write the protonation**
Add $\text{H}^+$ to the $\text{NH}_2$ to give $\text{NH}_3^+$. So $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CO}_2\text{Bu} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow [\text{H}_3\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CO}_2\text{Bu}]^+$. With $\text{HCl}$ this is the $\text{RNH}_3\text{Cl}$ salt.
Final answer: $\text{RNH}_2 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{RNH}_3^+$ where $\text{R}$ is the rest of butamben, or $\text{RNH}_2 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{RNH}_3\text{Cl}$.

hints: Compare the environment of the nitrogen lone pair in ammonia with that in an $\text{NH}_2$ group attached directly to a benzene ring.
walkthrough:
Compare availability of the lone pair**
In $\text{NH}_3$ the lone pair sits fully on nitrogen, ready to bond to $\text{H}^+$. In butamben the $\text{NH}_2$ is directly joined to benzene, just like phenylamine.

Use delocalisation to decide strength**
That lone pair overlaps with the pi system of the ring and is delocalised into it. Because it is partly drawn away, it is less readily donated to a proton, so butamben is a weaker base than ammonia.
Final answer: Weaker base than ammonia, because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and less available to accept $\text{H}^+$.

hints: Recall how a strongly activating $\text{NH}_2$ group directs $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ substitution on the ring.
Recall what $\text{HNO}_2$ with $\text{HCl}$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ does to a primary aromatic amine.
Recall what hot $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ does to an ester linkage.
walkthrough:
Bromination, activated ring**
The $\text{NH}_2$ group strongly activates the ring and is 2,4,6 directing. The 4 position is already blocked by the ester group, so substitution occurs at the two ortho positions to $\text{NH}_2$, which are the 3 and 5 positions relative to the ester. With excess $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ you get the 3,5-dibromo product, the ester side chain is unchanged.

Diazotisation, cold nitrous acid**
Primary aromatic amine plus $\text{HNO}_2$ made from $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$, kept at $0$ to $5^{\circ}\text{C}$, converts $\text{NH}_2$ to the diazonium group $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+$. So draw the same benzoate ester but replace $\text{H}_2\text{N-}$ para to the ester by $^+\text{N}\equiv\text{N-}$ para to the ester.

Alkaline hydrolysis of the ester**
Hot $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ cleaves esters by nucleophilic acyl substitution. The $\text{C(=O)-O}$ bond breaks to give the carboxylate salt and the alcohol. Here you get sodium 4-aminobenzoate, $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, plus butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. The amine does not react with $\text{NaOH}$.

Final answer: With $\text{Br}_2(aq)$: butyl 3,5-dibromo-4-aminobenzoate, $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_2\text{Br}_2\text{-C(=O)OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with Br at 3,5 positions relative to $\text{NH}_2$. With $\text{HNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$: diazonium salt, $[\text{N}\equiv\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C(=O)OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3]^+$. With $\text{NaOH}$ under reflux: $\text{H}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-C(=O)O}^-\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule to the butyl chain $\text{-OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and count which $\text{CH}_2$ or $\text{CH}_3$ groups have exactly two equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon.
walkthrough:
Apply n+1 to the butyl chain**
A triplet means n = 2 neighbouring protons. In $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$, the $\text{OCH}_2$ sees 2 H on the next $\text{CH}_2$, so n+1 = 3. The terminal $\text{CH}_3$ sees 2 H on the next $\text{CH}_2$, so n+1 = 3. The two middle $\text{CH}_2$ groups each see 4 or 5 neighbours, so they give larger multiplets. Hence exactly 2 triplet peaks.
Final answer: 2 peaks show a triplet splitting pattern.

hints: Focus on the two ends of the butyl chain, the $\text{CH}_2$ attached to oxygen and the $\text{CH}_3$ at the far end.
walkthrough:
Locate the two triplet groups**
On the labelled diagram, circle the two H atoms on the carbon directly bonded to O, that is $\text{C(=O)-O-CH}_2$. Then circle the three H atoms on the terminal carbon, that is $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3$. Those are the only groups with exactly two adjacent protons.
Final answer: Circle the $\text{OCH}_2$ protons ($\text{C(=O)OCH}_2$) and the terminal $\text{CH}_3$ protons ($\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$).

hints: Identify which protons in butamben are attached to N or O and are therefore labile.
Think about what happens when a labile $\text{N-H}$ proton meets $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ and whether deuterium gives a signal in proton NMR.
walkthrough:
Find the exchangeable protons**
Butamben has one $\text{NH}_2$ group. $\text{N-H}$ protons are labile, they can be transferred to solvent. All $\text{C-H}$ protons on the ring and butyl chain are non labile and stay put.

Explain the D2O shake effect**
In $\text{D}_2\text{O}$, $\text{R-NH}_2 + \text{D}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-ND}_2 + \text{HOD}$. Deuterium is a different isotope and does not resonate in the $^1\text{H}$ NMR region, so the $\text{NH}_2$ signal vanishes. The spectrum therefore has one less peak, all other peaks are essentially unchanged.

Final answer: One fewer peak in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$; the $\text{NH}_2$ peak disappears. The $\text{N-H}$ protons are labile and exchange with D from $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{ND}_2$ and HOD, and D does not appear in the proton NMR spectrum.

hints: Calculate the mass of a $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2$ unit and a $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$ unit and match them to m/e 92 and 57.
walkthrough:
Match masses to fragments**
Break the ester. The aromatic amine fragment $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2$ has mass $(6 \times 12) + (6 \times 1) + 14 = 92$, so $m/e$ 92 is $[\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{NH}_2]^+$. The butyl fragment $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$ has mass $(4 \times 12) + 9 = 57$, so $m/e$ 57 is $[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2]^+$. Both are common alpha cleavages around the ester group.
